summary: In this Thanksgiving episode of the Lord of Spirits, Fathers Andrew Stephen Damick and Stephen De Young discuss the Holy Eucharist, the second installment in their series on the Holy Mysteries of the Orthodox Church. They begin by addressing the question of whether the Eucharist is 'just a symbol,' firmly rejecting that notion and delving into the biblical and historical roots of the Eucharist as a sacrifice. They explore the Christian priesthood as a participation in Christ's priesthood, emphasizing that Christ is the true priest and His sacrifice is His voluntary self-offering. The hosts connect this to the Old Testament sacrificial system, particularly the sin offering, peace offering, and thank offering, and explain how the Eucharist gathers up these sacrifices. They also address the relationship between the Eucharist and the Jewish Passover, clarifying that the Last Supper was not a Seder but a pilgrimage meal, and that the Eucharist is a participation in Christ's once-for-all sacrifice, not a repetition. The second half of the episode includes listener voicemails on infant communion and the agape meal, and the third half focuses on the body and blood of Christ, discussing the prohibition on blood in the Old Testament, the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist, and the dangers of objectifying the sacrament. The episode concludes with practical exhortations to live a Eucharistic life, offering one's whole life to God.

entities.title: Jesus Christ
entities.summary: The central figure of Christianity, whose priesthood and sacrifice are the foundation of the Eucharist. He is the true priest and the offering.

entities.title: Melchizedek
entities.summary: King and priest of Jerusalem, who is a type of Christ. Christ is a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, which is a non-hereditary priesthood.

entities.title: Maccabean Martyrs
entities.summary: Jewish martyrs who offered themselves as sacrifices for their people, foreshadowing Christ's voluntary self-offering. Their stories are told in 2 and 4 Maccabees.

entities.title: St. Paul
entities.summary: Apostle who wrote 1 Corinthians, where he explicitly teaches that the Eucharist is a sacrifice and a participation in the body and blood of Christ.

entities.title: St. John
entities.summary: Author of the Gospel of John, which contains the Bread of Life discourse (John 6) and the account of the piercing of Christ's side, connecting the Eucharist to the creation of the Church.

entities.title: Passover
entities.summary: The Jewish feast commemorating the Exodus, which is a type of the Eucharist. The Eucharist is the new Passover, and Christ is the Passover lamb.

entities.title: Eucharist
entities.summary: The sacrament of the body and blood of Christ, which is a sacrifice, a meal, and a participation in Christ's self-offering. It is the central act of Christian worship.

entities.title: Orthodox Church
entities.summary: The Church that preserves the ancient faith, including the practice of infant communion and the understanding of the Eucharist as a sacrifice.

entities.title: Roman Catholic Church
entities.summary: The Western Church that developed the doctrine of transubstantiation and practices such as perpetual adoration, which are contrasted with the Orthodox approach.

entities.title: Protestantism
entities.summary: A movement that arose in the 16th century, often rejecting the sacrificial understanding of the Eucharist. The hosts critique the reactionary positions that stem from this period.

concepts.title: Christian Priesthood
concepts.summary: The Christian priesthood is not a continuation of the Levitical priesthood but a participation in Christ's priesthood. Christ is the one true priest, and human priests participate in His priesthood, offering the sacrifice of the Eucharist.

concepts.title: Eucharist as Sacrifice
concepts.summary: The Eucharist is a sacrifice, as explicitly taught by St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 10. It is a participation in Christ's self-offering, not a repetition or a mere memorial. The distinctions between sacrifice and meal, altar and table, are not biblically supportable.

concepts.title: Christ's Priesthood and Sacrifice
concepts.summary: Christ's priesthood is centered on His voluntary self-offering. He is both the priest and the victim, offering Himself to the Father. This is foreshadowed in the Jewish martyrs of the Maccabean period and fulfilled in Christ.

concepts.title: Eucharist and Passover
concepts.summary: The Eucharist has a special connection to the Passover, but it is not a Seder. The Last Supper was a pilgrimage meal, and the Eucharist is a participation in Christ's sacrifice, which fulfills the Passover. The use of leavened bread in the Eucharist signifies the resurrection.

concepts.title: Real Presence
concepts.summary: Christ is truly and really present in the Eucharist, regardless of the disposition of the recipient or the celebrant. The Orthodox Church does not define the 'how' of this presence, focusing instead on the transformative power of the sacrament.

concepts.title: Eucharist as Thanksgiving
concepts.summary: The word 'Eucharist' means 'thanksgiving,' and the sacrament is a thank offering to God. It is a participation in Christ's self-offering, which is the ultimate thank offering, and it includes elements of the Old Testament grain and drink offerings.

concepts.title: Infant Communion
concepts.summary: The Orthodox practice of giving communion to infants is rooted in the Passover, where the whole family participates. It reflects the belief that the Eucharist is nourishment for all, regardless of age or intellectual capacity, and that even infants can love God with their heart and soul.

concepts.title: Agape Meal
concepts.summary: The agape meal was a sacrificial meal that accompanied the Eucharist in the early Church, similar to the meals that accompanied Old Testament sacrifices. It was open to all, while the Eucharist was restricted to the faithful. The distinction highlights the sacrificial nature of the Eucharist.

concepts.title: Blood Prohibition
concepts.summary: The Old Testament prohibition on drinking blood was a limit on predation, reminding humanity not to become predatory. In the Eucharist, we drink Christ's blood, but it is not an act of predation; it is a voluntary self-offering that purifies us from sin.

concepts.title: Eucharist as Meal
concepts.summary: The Eucharist is a meal, but it is also a sacrifice. In the ancient world, sacrifices were meals, and the Eucharist is a sacrificial meal that brings us into communion with God and with one another.

claims.text: The Eucharist is not just a symbol; it is a real participation in the body and blood of Christ.
The Christian priesthood is a participation in Christ's priesthood, not a continuation of the Levitical priesthood.
The Eucharist is a sacrifice, as taught by St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 10, and it is a participation in Christ's self-offering.
The Last Supper was not a Seder; it was a pilgrimage meal, and the Eucharist is not a repetition of the Passover but a participation in Christ's once-for-all sacrifice.
The Eucharist is not a repetition of Christ's crucifixion; it is a participation in that one event, which is both historical and eternal.
Infants should receive the Eucharist because they are part of the family of God and can love God with their heart and soul, even without intellectual understanding.
The Old Testament prohibition on drinking blood was a limit on predation, reminding humanity not to become predatory.
The blood of Christ in the Eucharist purifies us from sin, not by appeasing wrath but by cleansing and transforming us.
Christ is present in the Eucharist regardless of the disposition of the recipient or the priest, which is why it can be harmful if received unworthily.
The Orthodox Church focuses on what the Eucharist does rather than defining the 'how' of Christ's presence, avoiding the Western debates on transubstantiation.

scriptural_links.summary: Quoted to establish Christ's priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek.
St. Paul explicitly links the Eucharist to sacrifice, comparing it to the sacrifices of Israel and pagan sacrifices to demons.
Used to show that the Greek word for 'memorial' is used for sacrifices, indicating that a memorial can be a sacrifice.
Describes the pilgrimage meal, which is the type of meal the Last Supper was.
The Bread of Life discourse, where Christ teaches that He is the bread of life and that we must eat His flesh and drink His blood.
The opening of Adam's side to create Eve is paralleled with the piercing of Christ's side, from which flow blood and water, creating the Church.
The piercing of Christ's side and the flow of blood and water, which are connected to the Eucharist and baptism.
The prohibition on blood applies to all Christians, but the Eucharist is an exception because it is Christ's voluntary self-offering.

glossary.definition: From the Greek 'eucharistia,' meaning 'thanksgiving.' The sacrament of the body and blood of Christ.
The Greek word for Passover, used by Orthodox Christians to refer to Easter, the feast of Christ's resurrection.
The Jewish ritual meal held on the first night of Passover, which developed after the destruction of the Temple.
The Roman Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ, with no trace of bread and wine remaining.
A view often associated with Lutheranism that the body and blood of Christ are present alongside the bread and wine.
A communal meal in the early Church that accompanied the Eucharist, open to all, while the Eucharist was restricted to the faithful.
Bread placed on a table in the tabernacle and temple, symbolizing God's presence and provision.
The bread from heaven that God provided for Israel in the wilderness, a type of the Eucharist.
